newsitem.title: USA: Clinton faces tough odds in battle for trade bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton faces tough odds in battle for trade bill.

text.p: President Bill Clinton faces an uphill battle with Congress to win new authority to negotiate trade agreements and the odds are running against him, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Thursday.

The administration has been talking with lawmakers to try to develop trade negotiation legislation that can win both Democratic and Republican votes. But Rubin told an investment group that obtaining so-called "fast track" trade negotiation authority "is going to be very difficult and the odds clearly are not in our favour."

Clinton needs fast-track trade authority to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) to include Chile and other agreements including a planned round of global talks on agriculture trade in 1999.

Rubin told the Investment Company Institute that fast track allows the president to negotiate trade agreements more effectively. Congress gives up the right to amend trade agreements and can only vote to accept or reject them.
Rubin said support for international engagement was shrinking in Congress.
"There are many who believe that NAFTA could not pass (the U.S. Congress) today," Rubin said. NAFTA links Canada, Mexico and the United States in a free trade zone.

Rubin told reporters that the administration would make a full-out effort to win passage of fast-track authority. Many supporters believe that the legislation will pass only with Clinton pushing for it fully.
Rubin noted that there are both supporters and opponents to fast track in both parties and that it will be difficult to win the votes for passage.

Sens. Byron Dorgan, Democrat of North Dakota, and Olympia Snowe, a Maine Republican, announced on Thursday they would vote against fast-track authority because they believe that NAFTA has not benefited the United States and has led to an erosion of Americans' standard of living.

Those views were underscored at a hearing held by the U.S. International Trade Commission which has been asked by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky to study the impact of NAFTA on the U.S. economy.

"It clearly has not been good for workers," Gregory Woodhead, an AFL-CIO economist, told the panel. He cited a rapid rise in the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico under the agreement, job loss from manfacturing moving south and increased downward wage pressures experienced by workers.
He also cited a Cornell University study that showed large numbers of U.S. employers have used the threat of closing plants and moving operations to Mexico to thwart union organising drives.

But business groups anxious to bring Chile into NAFTA and eventually form an Americas trading bloc urgently want fast track. They argue that NAFTA has been good for the U.S. economy and that the United States will be left behind as competitors in Japan and Europe form new trade relationships with Latin American countries, a traditional market for U.S. exporters.

The administration has been without fast-track authority since 1994 and efforts to win new trade negotiation legislation have been bogged down in a dispute between Republicans and Democrats over authority to include labour and environmental issues in trade deals.
The administration has yet to send Congress proposed legislation, saying they are trying to work out a bill that will win both Democratic and Republican support.

The chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, Bill Archer, Republican of Texas, told Clinton in a letter on Thursday that the delay is making it impossible for Congress to consider legislation on a timely basis.
"There comes a time when the preparatory work must end and we move ahead, especially when the congressinal schedule requires such timely action," he said.
